W., 'A Semantic Basis for Local Reasoning', FoSSaCS 2002, LNCS 2303, pp. 402-416, doi:10.1007/3-540-45931-6_28 (author PDF http://www0.cs.ucl.ac.uk/staff/p.ohearn/papers/basis.pdf). Section 4: Lemma 1 (Safety and Termination Monotonicity), Lemma 2 (Frame Property), Theorem 1 (soundness of the Frame Rule, with the side condition that the command modifies no variable free in the frame). Section 4.1: an operation that traps memory faults would let a program branch on whether a cell is active, contradicting Safety Monotonicity; and an abstract setting is sketched in which an arbitrary partial commutative monoid replaces heaps, with a local action defined as a relation satisfying Safety and Termination Monotonicity and the Frame Property, for which 'the Frame Rule is sound for every local action' (no cancellativity is required).

Published package 'frame-rule-locality-and-precise-assertions' of this corpus (google/zerocopy branch reference, commit 8ff18039787575ce7f24066acdc7600918ad8185). Its definitions of separation structures, commands, outcomes, assertions, separating conjunction, fault-avoiding triples, SafetyMono, FrameProp, Local and FrameRuleSound (support file lean/Toy/Sep/Basic.lean, namespace Toy.Sep) are the source of this package's lean/Toy/ByteSL/SepBasic.lean, which consists of a subset of that file's declarations, their code copied unchanged and the namespace renamed to Toy.ByteSL. Its R2b (Toy.Sep.frameRuleSound_iff_safetyMono_and_frameProp: in any separation structure, no laws, FrameRuleSound c <-> SafetyMono c and FrameProp c) is the same statement as R5a here; its R5 shows lookup, mutation, allocation and deallocation local in a finite-heap model with arbitrary cell values, address-disjoint union and no permissions; its R3a-R3d exhibit non-local heap commands (an allocation test, fixed-address allocation that faults, least-free-address allocation, predictable allocation).
design_question: A verifier for low-level Rust wants byte-level ownership (padding, uninitialized memory, reinterpretation) together with typed reasoning: which typed points-to to build from byte points-to, when struct ownership splits into field ownership with padding, when a transmute is a pure view change, and how read-only views interact with these.

tier_justification: The permission algebra is COY 2007's {R, RW} (Definition 1, Example 2); that idempotent sharing makes the induced heap algebra non-cancellative is immediate (h * h = h * emp) and is why later treatments keep cancellativity separate (Klein-Kolanski-Boyton's Isabelle library has a separate cancellative subclass). Restated here.
plain_claim: For every byte payload type D, the byte heap with read-only sharing is a partial commutative monoid with unit (symmetric disjointness, commutativity, partial associativity, the empty heap as unit) but is not right-cancellative: the read-only cell 0 |-> uninit is disjoint from itself and from the empty heap, and combined with itself gives the same heap as the empty heap combined with it, although it is not the empty heap.
nonvacuity_witness: The counterexample itself.
non_claims: Does not affect R5a, which needs no algebraic law; results that depend on cancellativity (for example relating precision to the conjunction rule) do not transfer to this heap without further argument.

Idempotent read-only sharing violates the disjointness axiom of Dockins, Hobor and Appel (2009): a separating conjunction of read-only assertions does not imply that their footprints are disjoint (two read-only views of the same cells separate, R4a). Inductive predicates built with * at permission ro (lists, trees) therefore admit sharing and cycles (DAGs instead of trees); nothing here supports reading ro-separation as address disjointness.

Permissions are the two-point permission algebra full | read-only (read-only cells combine idempotently with equal cells, full cells with nothing); there are no fractions, so nothing here addresses splitting full ownership into read-only pieces or recombining them.

Toy model: one flat byte heap with natural-number addresses, no allocation, no alignment, no provenance in the examples, no lifetimes or borrows, no concurrency; a representation's decoder depends on the bytes only.
prior_art: Calcagno, C., O'Hearn, P. W. & Yang, H., 'Local Action and Abstract Separation Logic', LICS 2007, pp. 366-378, doi:10.1109/LICS.2007.30 (author PDF http://www0.cs.ucl.ac.uk/staff/p.ohearn/papers/asl-short.pdf): Section 3 recalls Safety Monotonicity and the Frame Property for relations and states that 'a relation R satisfies Safety Monotonicity and the Frame Property iff the frame rule is sound for it'. Definition 1 takes a separation algebra to be a cancellative partial commutative monoid; its Example 2 (heaps with permissions, HPerm, over a permission algebra required to be cancellative) mentions the permission algebra {R, RW} with R o R = R and RW o p undefined, remarking that it does not allow converting a total (RW) permission into several read permissions or back. That two-point algebra is the permission algebra of this package; the heap algebra it induces with the empty heap as unit is not cancellative (R5f), so this instance lies outside Definition 1.

Klein, G., Kolanski, R. & Boyton, A., 'Mechanised Separation Algebra', ITP 2012, LNCS 7406, pp. 332-337, doi:10.1007/978-3-642-32347-8_22, with the Archive of Formal Proofs entry 'Separation Algebra' (May 2012): an Isabelle/HOL type-class library of separation algebras based on COY 2007 in which cancellativity is a separate subclass (cancellative_sep_algebra, assumption sep_add_cancelD: x + z = y + z with x ## z and y ## z implies x = y), the right-cancellation law RightCancel of this package.

Gotsman, A., Berdine, J. & Cook, B., 'Precision and the Conjunction Rule in Concurrent Separation Logic', Electronic Notes in Theoretical Computer Science 276 (MFPS XXVII), pp. 171-190, 2011, doi:10.1016/j.entcs.2011.09.021: studies the interplay of precision and the conjunction rule in separation logic, the kind of result that does not transfer to non-cancellative models without further argument (cited for its topic only).

Dockins, R., Hobor, A. & Appel, A. W., 'A Fresh Look at Separation Algebras and Share Accounting', APLAS 2009, LNCS 5904, pp. 161-177, doi:10.1007/978-3-642-10672-9_13 (author PDF https://www.cs.princeton.edu/~appel/papers/fresh-sa.pdf): revisits the separation-algebra axioms; its disjointness axiom (a + a = b implies a = b: no nonempty share joins with itself) is motivated by the remark that without disjointness 'the obvious definition of a formula to describe binary trees in fact describes directed acyclic graphs'. The idempotent read-only cells of this package violate that axiom.

Vindum, S. F. & Birkedal, L., 'Contextual Refinement of the Michael-Scott Queue (Proof Pearl)', CPP 2021, pp. 76-90, doi:10.1145/3437992.3439930: introduces discardable fractions for Iris points-to assertions, where a fraction can be irrevocably discarded to obtain persistent, freely duplicable read-only ownership; Iris itself is described in Jung, R., Krebbers, R., Jourdan, J.-H., Bizjak, A., Birkedal, L. & Dreyer, D., 'Iris from the ground up', Journal of Functional Programming 28, e20, 2018, doi:10.1017/S0956796818000151. The read-only permission of this package behaves like a discarded fraction without the fractional part.

Boyland, J., 'Checking Interference with Fractional Permissions', SAS 2003, LNCS 2694, pp. 55-72, doi:10.1007/3-540-44898-5_4: introduces fractional permissions (writing needs the whole permission, reading any fraction; fractions recombine). Cited as the origin of fractional permissions; the two-point full / read-only algebra here is a non-fractional, non-recombinable variant.
